Ecosystem Modelling Suitability Assessment

The University of the Sunshine Coast offers some students the opportunity to complete a special research project under an academic supervisor as a part of their undergraduate. The project runs over a 10 week period with approximately 100 hours of dedicated study on a topic co-designed between the student and supervisor.

Project Overview:

The goal of the project was to investigate Rpath, an R package that uses bioenergetics to model energy flows within ecosystems, for its suitability at modelling marine ecosystems. A preliminary investigation of the package's capabilities was conducted to determine suitability for a future research project investigating how perturbations from several climate change scenarios would impact a model marine ecosystem.

Key Objectives:

The the research project required me to perform several key objectives and deliverables by the end of the study period.

Including:

  • To describe and showcase Rpath's capabilities
  • Investigate resources for learning and teaching Rpath
  • Determine modelling data requirements and identify potential data sources
  • Identify key barriers and limitations to model use

Skills developed:

This project allowed me to develop skills in independent research, note-taking, technical writing, as well as project and time management. Weekly progress updates to my supervisor required detailed note-taking and time-management for accurate presentation during the projects run-time. I also further developed my coding skills in R and gained considerable knowledge on trophic webs and their use in fishery management.



A George Banks model plot of the relative biomass over time for a marine ecosystem. From Link et al.(2006)

Project Outcomes:

The final findings of the suitability assessment were presented at the end of the study period in a detailed report accompanied by a presentation. It was assessed that the model technique shows considerable value for fishery management and research but has large data requirements that can be difficult to procure, particularly given the lack of open-source availability of data between researchers.

The report also noted that model validation was a key but under-used faculty despite readily available resources made accessible by the model developers, indicating a variation in the quality of models being produced using the framework. It is expected that with the adoption of the Ecopath framework to R that ecologists are likely to incorporate the system into their fishery management workflows, extending collaboration and package development.
